analytic.title: MSOF-DT Strategy and Its Impact on Real-Time Systems Scheduling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: When managing Real-Time System execution, dynamic deadlines are problems that are not easy to handle. If a real-time computation is built using the traditional approach (Run-to-Completion), then there is no tolerance for the time of completion of the execution. Using the MSOF-DT computation strategy, the RT task can be more tolerant of the reduced processing time (deadline changes). Besides that, in this paper, we also propose a real-time process scheduling algorithm based on the MSOF-DT strategy, called EDSEF/MSOF-DT. The schedulability of the schedule produced by EDSEF/MSOF-DT can be better than the schedule generated by the EDF algorithm and also higher than using (Min_D + Min_C) policy alone without MSOF-DT, both in cases without interruptions or cases that contain interruptions.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In Real-Time Systems (RTS), the accuracy of the results and the time of presentation of the results are the two main aspects that determine the effectiveness or success of computing. In other words, a Real-Time System is a computer-based system that must meet both logical correctness requirements and temporal constraints. [1] [2]. For most of the cases, Real-Time Systems do not operate as standalone systems, instead, they interact with other systems that act as data generator/providers and systems that act as users of the results/responses [3] In general, Real-Time Systems can be classified into three types, namely: soft, hard, and firm. Soft Real-Time Systems are systems whose performance is considered to decrease (but not fatal) if they fail to meet the time constraint. If a hard Real-Time System fails to meet the deadline (even just once), then the system is considered a total failure and may result in disaster. On the other hand, a firm Real-Time System tolerates several (small) deadline violations, but if there are more violations than that amount, the system is considered a failure [2]. While Laplante defines a firm Real-Time System by tolerating deadline violations (with a small probability) while still trying to maintain the correctness of computational results, Liu et al. provide a different definition, namely by giving tolerance to the reduction in the quality of computational results (to a certain extent) so that the results can be presented on time or do not violate deadlines [4].

So far, the available literature has provided explanations regarding techniques to increase the chances of completion of execution without violating deadlines, for example by using various scheduling algorithms. However, no one has presented a discussion related to cases of execution with deadlines that may experience changes (dynamic deadlines) for a real-time task. Deadlines might change or the allocation of processing time could be shortened due to interruptions.

The approaches used in the existing researches aimed to improve computation performance usually focus on efforts to produce outcomes that have very high accuracy and try to shorten the completion time of execution of all parts of the computation. Computation cannot be considered finished before all processes are run and/or all data is processed. Schwarzfischer calls this kind of approach as Run-to-Completion (RtC) [5].

In some of our previous studies [6] [7] [8] [9], a new approach has been proposed to improve computational effectiveness, called Run-to-Decisive (RtD). In this approach, the calculations are carried out only up to a condition where the results of the calculation have been able/sufficient to be used in making correct decisions (have reached a decisive state). Based on this approach, the Most Significant Operation First -Double Track (MSOF-DT) computation strategy has been proposed. The main ideas of the strategy are: 1) arrange the order of execution according to the significance of each computational element, 2) perform calculations to obtain intermediate results in the form of lower bound and upper bound, 3) use both of the lower bound and upper bound to make an intermediate decision, and 4) stop the execution when the decisive conditions have been reached.

In this paper, the MSOF-DT strategy is used to increase the tolerance of the Real-Time Systems (especially in dealing with dynamic deadlines) and is also used to develop a new real-time process scheduling algorithm. The contents of this paper are as follows: right after the introduction section, a summary of the MSOF-DT strategy is given in chapter II, the next chapter introduces how MSOF-DT strategy provides benefits to RTS, the new RTS scheduling algorithm and it's simulation are presented in chapter IV, finally the last chapter contains the conclusion.

div.head: II. SUMMARY OF MSOF-DT STRATEGY
div.p: Execution of computation whose elements are sorted by significance is expected to provide an increase in the quality of the results as quickly as possible. By first working on the more important elements (greater contribution to the final result), it is expected that the accuracy of the calculation results can be increased more quickly, or in other words, the uncertainty range of the results can shrink faster.

The use of lower bound and dynamic upper bound aims to narrow the range of uncertainty faster. Lower and upper bounds are values that limit the range of probable actual values of the final calculation results. These two values also indicate the uncertainty range of the final results of the calculation. Lower bound at time t can be an intermediate value obtained from the result of execution until time t. The upper bound at time t can be the upper bound of the initial (at the beginning of the calculation) minus the lower bound at t. Because we deal with computation which has non-decreasing monotonic properties, the lower bound also has nondecreasing monotonic properties. Whereas the upper bound will have non-increasing monotonic properties. This dynamic upper bound makes the range of uncertainty narrower more quickly than using a static upper bound. These two boundary values are then used in decision making and compared with the decision criteria. If the decision obtained at that time is convincing enough (reaching the decisive state), then the execution can be stopped. The execution of the remaining processes and/or the remaining data can be ignored because it will not change the final decision obtained at that time. (time tc) we have the real calculation result and the correct decision "B" since all of the computation elements have been executed (run-to-completion). Using the MSOF-DT strategy, we check the decisiveness in every step or iteration. At tb, the lower bound and the upper bound lied in the same decision class "B", which means we have correct decision earlier than tc. We can stop the execution at tb and have the advantages of time-saving (tc -tb). To handle incremental computational elements, there are six parts of this MSOF-DT computation strategy, namely: 1) determination of significance, 2) sequencing of computation elements, 3) calculation/execution of computation elements, 4) calculation of the lower bound and upper bound, 5) decision making, and 6) examination of decisive conditions and deadlines. Every time a decision is needed, first sort the level of significance of all computing elements. Then the execution/calculation is carried out in the order of their significance to produce a lower bound value and an upper bound value. The boundary values are then used for decision making using established criteria. If a decision cannot be obtained (decisive conditions have not yet been reached) and the time is still available, and execution is carried out for the next computational element. Iteration of calculation -decision making continues until a decision can be determined [9]. How MSOF-DT works can be visualized by a flowchart as shown in Fig. 2.

div.head: III. MSOF-DT AND REAL-TIME SYSTEM
div.p: Using the MSOF-DT strategy, the time to get the correct results or to reach a decisive condition (tdecisive) can be faster than the time needed to run all computational elements (tcomplete). In Fig. 3 the width of the period between tcomplete and tdecisive shows how wide the execution time tolerance the process has. To show how much time savings obtained from the use of a particular computational strategy (in this case is MSOF-DT) compared to the use of conventional strategies (which executes all computational elements), the Time-to-Decisive Saving (TtDS) metric can be used. TtDS is formulated as follows:

TtD: time-to-decisive, the time required by a computation (with certain strategies) to achieve the decisive condition TtC: time-to-completion, the time needed to execute all parts of the computation By using the Run-to-Completion paradigm, tdecisive will always coincide with the tcomplete so that the TtDS value is 0. Using the MSOF-DT strategy, tdecisive can be smaller than tcomplete so that the TtDS value can be greater than 0.

Tolerance to the narrower processing time limit will provide benefits for the Real-Time System. The greater the system's tolerance to the shortening of the process time allocation, the better the system is. Greater tolerance will increase the chance of not violating deadlines. Although the allocation of processing time is reduced (for example due to interruptions) and has to be stopped before all operations are performed or all data is processed, as long as the execution exceeds the time required to reach the decisive condition, the current result can be declared as correct and acceptable one (obtaining accomplished status).

div.head: IV. THE EDSEF/MSOF-DT SCHEDULING ALGORITHM
div.p: In the Real-Time Systems research area, the process scheduling algorithm is an interesting topic. The main purpose of the real-time process scheduling algorithm is to meet the specification of response time requirements and to increase the value of schedulability [2]. Schedulability of a set of tasks scheduled using a certain scheduling algorithm can be expressed as a ratio between the number of tasks that can be scheduled and completed without violating the deadline with the total number of tasks entering the scheduling system. The more processes that can be scheduled and completed without violating the deadline, the better the scheduling algorithm is.

One important component in the scheduling algorithm is the priority assignment policy. One popular policy is Min_D, which is used in the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) classic scheduling algorithm. This Min_D policy prioritizes tasks that have the smallest / earliest deadlines. Besides Min_D, there are also some other policies. Policies that involve deadlines and runtime are Min_D + Min_C [10], in this paper, we call it the Earliest Deadline and Shortest Execution Time First (EDSEF). This policy is a combination of two policies, namely: Min_D (Pr (τ) = D) and Min_C (prioritizing the task that has the shortest processing time; Pr (τ) = C). By using the MSOF-DT strategy, real-time processes have the opportunity to be completed without having to execute all the elements. div.head: Algorithm: EDSEF/MSOF-DT (no interrupt)
div.p:
The EDSEF/MSOF-DT algorithm above can be enriched with the ability to handle interruptions that can come at any time and are considered to have the highest priority for immediate execution (can interrupt the currently running tasks). The modified algorithm becomes as shown in Fig 8 .
Algorithm: EDSEF/MSOF-DT (with interrupt) As an example, one interrupt task is added to the task specification in Table 2 so that it becomes as written in Table 3. It appears that the priority (Pr(τ)) of the interrupt has the smallest value of all other tasks. Consequently, the interrupt task must be run immediately and it will interrupt the currently running task (task D). If the task set in Table 3 is scheduled using the EDF algorithm (Min_D policy), the following schedule is obtained: Using EDSEF/MSOF-DT, all tasks are successfully executed, which gives schedulability = 4/4. The schedulability value is higher than using Min_D only (EDF algorithm).

To find out more about how the EDSEF / MSOF-DT scheduling algorithm performs on a larger number of tasks, a Real-Time scheduling simulation is performed. This simulation uses Cheddar (a free real-time scheduling simulator from http://beru.univ-brest.fr/~singhoff/cheddar/). In this simulation, three scheduling algorithms are compared, namely: EDF (using Min_D policy), EDSEF (using Min_D + Min_C policy), and EDSEF / MSOF-DT (using Min_D + Min_C policy plus MSOF-DT strategy). The number of tasks that enter the system is = {5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 35}, with processing time and deadlines determined randomly. The TtDS value for each task follows a uniform random distribution between 0% and 80%. Some interrupt tasks are inserted randomly. It appears that for all the number of tasks used in the simulation, the EDSEF / MSOF-DT algorithm gives a higher schedulability value (more tasks that are successfully executed and accomplished) than either the EDF algorithm or EDSEF algorithm. The decline in the value of schedulability as the number of tasks increases is a natural phenomenon. An increasing number of tasks that go into the system and compete for the scheduled task will reduce opportunities to be executed and completed without violating the deadline.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: The MSOF-DT strategy that can minimize the number of operations (and processing time) while still providing the correct results has been implemented to increase the tolerance of the Real-Time System so that it is more resilient in handling dynamic deadlines. This strategy has also opened up opportunities for developing real-time scheduling algorithms, so that real-time processes have a greater chance of being able to be completed despite a reduction in time allocation (for example: because there is an interrupt). It has also been shown that the schedulability of the schedule generated by the EDSEF / MSOF-DT algorithm can be higher than the schedule generated by the EDF algorithm and also higher than using (Min_D + Min_C) policy alone without MSOF-DT.
